entries.meaning: Knowing this in your heart, brother, Rāma said, serve the feet of our mother and father. Bharata and Śatrughna are away, the king is old, and my departure weighs upon his mind. If I go to the forest and take you, Ayodhyā will be orphaned in every respect; teacher, father, mother, subjects, and household will all bear an unbearable burden of grief. Remain and satisfy them all, dear brother, or a grave fault will result. A king whose beloved subjects suffer is certainly fit for hell. Consider this policy and remain. Hearing it, Lakṣmaṇa was overwhelmed; like a lotus touched by frost, he withered beneath those cooling words. Love left him no answer, and he clutched Rāma's feet in anguish: Lord, I am your servant and you are my master—what dwelling can there be for me if you abandon me?

Lakṣmaṇa said that Rāma had given him excellent teaching, but it was inaccessible to one of his own timidity and dependence. Such instruction belonged to resolute, noble men who bore the burden of dharma and were qualified in scriptural ethics. He was only a child raised in his lord's affection: could Mount Mandara or Meru be carried by a swan? He knew no teacher, father, mother, or anyone else; he spoke from his very nature and asked Rāma to believe him. Every love, relationship, confidence, and affection recognized by scripture was centered for him in Rāma alone—his sole master, friend of the lowly, and knower within the heart. Teach dharma and policy to one who values fame, prosperity, and blessed destiny; how could the ocean of compassion abandon one devoted in thought, deed, word, and feet? Hearing his brother's humble, loving words, Rāma embraced and reassured the fearful Lakṣmaṇa.

Rāma told Lakṣmaṇa to seek leave from his mother and return quickly so they might go to the forest together. At these words he rejoiced: a great gain had come and a great loss departed. Glad at heart, he went to his mother like a blind man whose sight had been restored, bowed his head at her feet, though his mind was already with Rāma and Jānakī, and answered her troubled question by recounting everything. Hearing the harsh news, Sumitrā recoiled like a doe surrounded by forest fire. Lakṣmaṇa saw that disaster threatened: overcome by affection, she might obstruct what had to be done. He asked leave timidly and hesitantly, wondering whether destiny would allow him to accompany Rāma. Then Sumitrā recalled Rāma and Sītā's beauty, character, and nature; seeing the king's love, she shook her head at the sinful woman who had made this cruel turn.

Recognizing the painful hour, Sumitrā mastered herself and spoke with the gentle voice of a natural friend: Dear son, Vaidehī is your mother and Rāma, who loves you in every way, your father. Ayodhyā is wherever Rāma dwells, just as day exists wherever the sun shines. If Sītā and Rāma go to the forest, you have no purpose in Ayodhyā. Teacher, father, mother, kinsman, deity, and master are all to be served like life itself, yet all are most worthy and dear precisely through their relation to Rāma. Knowing this within, go with them to the forest and gain the world's true reward of life. I count myself greatly blessed, together with you, if your heart has taken its place at Rāma's feet without deceit.

Only that woman in the world is truly a mother whose son is a devotee of Rāma; otherwise barrenness is better than bearing a son averse to him. It is through your good fortune that Rāma is going to the forest, dear one; there is no other cause. The greatest fruit of all merit is natural affection for the feet of Rāma and Sītā. Never, even in a dream, fall under attachment, anger, jealousy, pride, or delusion. Abandon every fault and serve them in thought, deed, and word. The forest will be thoroughly comfortable for you, for your father and mother—Rāma and Sītā—are there. Act so that Rāma suffers no hardship: this alone is my counsel, and let Ayodhyā's pleasures and its dear people fade from memory in their happiness. Sumitrā blessed him with ever-new, stainless love for their feet. Lakṣmaṇa bowed and departed at once, relieved at heart like a deer that has broken a perilous snare and runs under destiny's favor.

Lakṣmaṇa reached the place where Sītā's lord stood, rejoicing to have gained his beloved company. Bowing to Rāma and Sītā's lovely feet, he went with them to the royal palace. The townspeople said among themselves that Fate had arranged matters well only to spoil them. Their bodies were wasted, their faces dim, and their minds frantic like flies robbed of honey. They wrung their hands and beat their heads, distressed like birds without wings. A vast crowd filled the royal court with immeasurable grief. The minister raised the king and seated him; after tender words Rāma stepped forward. Seeing both handsome sons with Sītā, the lord of the earth was utterly overwhelmed and repeatedly drew them to his heart.

The anguished king could not speak, for grief had kindled a terrible fire within his heart. Bowing his head with deep devotion, Rāma rose and asked leave, requesting his father's blessing and command. Why turn a joyful occasion into bewilderment, he asked; if a father lets affection cause a lapse from duty, his fame is lost and reproach spreads through the world. Overcome by love, the king rose, took Rāma by the arms, and seated him again. He said that sages declared Rāma lord of all moving and unmoving creation, and that the Supreme gives the fruit appropriate to each person's good and evil action. Everyone says that whoever performs an act receives its fruit—yet one commits an offense and another bears its painful result. Who in the world is capable of understanding the Lord's exceedingly strange course?

The king honestly tried many ways to keep Rāma back, but the wise and steadfast bearer of dharma saw Rāma's resolve and knew he would not remain. Then the king clasped Sītā to his breast and lovingly instructed her at length, describing the forest's unbearable hardships and explaining the comfort afforded by parents-in-law and her father. Sītā's mind, however, was attached to Rāma's feet; home did not seem easy, nor forest difficult. Everyone else also tried to persuade her by magnifying the woods' dangers. The minister's wife and the wise wife of the family teacher spoke with tender affection: no exile had been imposed upon her, so she should do as father-in-law, teacher, and mother-in-law advised. Their cool, beneficial, sweet counsel did not please Sītā; it distressed her like autumn moonlight falling upon a cakravāka bird.

Bound by modesty, Sītā made no reply. Hearing the exchange, Kaikeyī sprang up irritably, brought vessels, ornaments, and ascetic garments, set them down before Rāma, and spoke with feigned gentleness. She said the king loved Rāma as his very life and, because of his character and affection, could not put aside his timidity; no one would ask him to go after destroying merit, good name, and the next world, so he should reflect and do as he wished. Rāma's mother found comfort in his counsel, but Kaikeyī's words struck the king like arrows, and the unfortunate monarch still could not die. The people were distraught and the king fainted, leaving no one able to think what to do. Rāma promptly put on the hermit's dress, bowed to his parents, and prepared to depart with his wife, brother, and all the forest gear. After reverencing brahmins and his teacher's feet, he left everyone almost senseless.

Passing out through Vasiṣṭha's gate, Rāma stood where he saw the people scorched by the forest fire of separation. With loving words he consoled them all and summoned the assembled brahmins. He bestowed maintenance upon them and, through reverence, gifts, and humility, placed himself under their goodwill. Petitioners were satisfied with gifts and honor, and pure-hearted friends with love. He called the male and female servants, entrusted them to his teacher, and with joined hands begged him to care for them like parents. Again and again Rāma joined his palms and gently told everyone that whoever acted for his true welfare would keep the king at ease. He asked the supremely wise citizens to find every means by which none of his mothers would become miserable and destitute through separation from him.
